question: Does an isolated-family kernel win transfer to the production token?
change: two-pass argmax: the incumbent launches grid(256) TG(256) -- ONE threadgroup of 256 threads to scan 248,320 logits, so each thread walks ~970 entries serially and 59 of 60 cores idle. The replacement fans pass 1 across 240 threadgroups and reduces the partials in pass 2, preserving the lower-index tie-break exactly at every level.
correctness: greedy token ids IDENTICAL to the serial kernel on all 16 tokens, oracle True, fallbacks 0, in every run

end_to_end_paired.arms: HAWKING_ARGMAX_TWO_PASS 0 vs 1, alternating, same session conditions

verdict: NO TRANSFER. A 26x kernel speedup worth 0.326 ms in isolation -- 5.6% of the entire non-GEMV wall -- produces a median end-to-end delta of -0.045 ms, which is nothing, and the two-pass arm is marginally SLOWER. Default left OFF: a second dispatch and two buffers for an unmeasurable win is not worth shipping.
why_it_matters: G110 and G111 are census-driven: measure the isolated families, retile the worst, expect the token to fall. That worked for gated_delta -- 3.38 ms isolated became 3.34 ms end to end, nearly 1:1 -- and it did NOT work here. So isolated-family time is a RANKING signal, not a budget: a family's isolated cost is an upper bound on what removing it can buy, and for small families the realisable fraction can be zero. Every retile must be paired end-to-end, which is what G111's acceptance already demands and this is the case that shows why.
one_real_side_effect: the two-pass arm is far more STABLE: spread 0.060 ms against 0.281. Not a speed win, but it makes the token wall easier to measure, which matters for every future A/B.
